extracted.intended_audience: artists, art historians, and general readers interested in Renaissance painting and sculpture
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical criteria for producing and judging excellence in Renaissance painting and sculpture (technical, compositional, material, moral, and professional standards) as presented in Vasari's artist biographies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief and force combined with delicacy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Pictures which have no relief and force, combined with delicacy, are of no account."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work should achieve both strength (relief/force) and delicacy together. Vasari illustrates this with Mariotto's Annunciation where figures stand out in strong relief against a dark background while maintaining graceful delicacy. Avoid flat, delicate pictures lacking force; likewise, avoid heavy shadows that destroy delicacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shadow/shading balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Shadows must not be so dark as to remain indistinct, nor so delicate as to lack force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shadows to give relief without losing clarity. Vasari notes the difficulty of making shadows dark enough to create relief but delicate enough to retain detail; artists should seek methods to combine both (Mariotto repeatedly reworked colouring to achieve this).

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric/pictorial perspective by tonal modulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distant views should be made to recede by lowering the tones; nearer elements can be brought forward by lightening them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on-site (e.g., install windows) to judge recession; intentionally lower tones for high/distant parts of a view and heighten nearer tones to create depth. Example: Mariotto had special windows to work on the spot to control receding views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative refinement and reworking
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter should repeatedly change and rework colouring and passages until satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari describes Mariotto painting out and repainting many times, varying colours and light/dark to achieve the intended expression. Iteration is a valued part of the process rather than a sign of failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursuit and mastery of pigments/highlights
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek brighter, more brilliant whites and refine pigments (e.g., clarify lead-white) to heighten highest lights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with materials and preparation to achieve the desired luminosity in highlights; Vasari recounts a painter attempting to clarify lead-white to obtain superior brilliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draughtsmanship and facility in perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellent drawing and a good knowledge of perspective are foundational to the arts of design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long, diligent study in drawing and imitation of excellent works is required. Vasari cites many drawings by Raffaellino and Visino (e.g., spiral staircase) as evidence of the importance of perspective and strong draftsmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery across media and techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to work skillfully in multiple media (fresco, distemper, oil, chiaroscuro drawing, terra-cotta, marble, bronze) is a mark of ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari notes painters who excel in distemper, fresco, and oils and sculptors who work in terra-cotta, marble, and bronze. Versatility and competence in each chosen medium are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex, expressive composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures should be varied, spirited, and expressive; complex groupings and contrivances (e.g., ladders and multiple postures) demonstrate skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Visino's Christ taken down from the Cross with varied, fantastic attitudes and complicated arrangements proves his ability. Composition should serve the narrative and show control of many figures in space.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-site observation and working from nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Work on the actual spot or from observation to control optical effects and perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mariotto had special windows made to work on-site so he could modulate tones for recession and bring elements forward; direct observation is recommended to judge spatial effects accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and imitation of ancient statuary (antique models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study of antique sculpture and copying classical works is essential training and a school of excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lorenzo's garden of antiquities served as an academy for students; Vasari argues that long imitation and study of ancient models accelerates and deepens artistic formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long course of study and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts can only be acquired by long study in drawing and diligent imitation of excellent works; natural talent alone is insufficient without training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari emphasizes patient practice and imitation as the only reliable path to perfection; youthful zeal helps but requires sustained study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance and moral conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist must be temperate and avoid worldly pleasures, as study and pleasures seldom agree together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari states that the arts call for a vigorous, awake mind and that those given to worldly delights should avoid serious study; moral discipline is part of professional success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and physical fitness for practice
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level painting and sculpture require a vigorous mind and steady hand; older craftsmen whose hands tremble should give advice rather than attempt arduous work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari counsels that the arts demand youthful vigour for execution and that elder masters are better employed in teaching or advising when manual steadiness declines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional conduct: avoid envy, destruction, and quarrels
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists must not allow envy or violent temper to damage careers or works of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari recounts Torrigiano's envy leading to violent acts (breaking Michelangelo's nose, spoiling others' works) and ultimate ruin; good conduct and collegiality are implicit professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and patronage conditions affect quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Poverty, heavy family burdens, or accepting mean wages can cause deterioration of an artist's work; patron support and fair payment enable excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari notes Raffaellino's decline when forced to accept low-paid work to provide for family, and praises Lorenzo's patronage of young talent as enabling many masters to flourish. Patrons supporting study and rewarding excellence bring honour to themselves and the arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care and craftsmanship even in 'minor' works
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs for embroidery, hangings, or small-scale works deserve careful draughtsmanship and diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when reduced to designing for embroidery, Raffaellino produced beautiful designs that proved his skill; minor commissions should still exhibit careful workmanship and creativity.
